segments.text: A Continuous-Time Causal Graph Learning Framework for Predicting and Mitigating Cascading Failures in Global Supply Chains Abstract-Global supply chains face increasing exposure to rapidly propagating disruptions triggered by geopolitical conflicts, climate-related shocks, and operational instabilities. Existing predictive approaches, including recent causal graph neural networks, remain limited by static causal structures, discrete-time reasoning, and post-hoc counterfactual analysis. These constraints reduce their ability to anticipate high-velocity cascade effects and to recommend proactive, cost-effective interventions. This work introduces CT-SCaLE, a novel Continuous-Time Structural Causal Learning Engine that unifies Neural ODE-based temporal dynamics, end-to-end differentiable causal structure learning, and counterfactual contrastive representation learning into a single predictive and decision-support architecture. CT-SCaLE learns both the evolving causal topology and the temporal propagation dynamics of disruptions, allowing the model to capture time-varying influences, multi-tier propagation patterns, and realistic feedback loops that traditional DAG-based causal GNNs cannot represent. Evaluations on SupplyGraph and Time-Series Risk datasets show that CT-SCaLE improves disruption prediction accuracy by up to 14.7%, increases early-warning lead time by 22%, and reduces simulated cascade size under optimized interventions by 31.4%, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines.
segments.label: human

segments.text: A key contribution is an embedded model-based intervention planner that performs multi-step counterfactual simulations to identify the minimum-cost actions capable of suppressing or redirecting cascading failures. This addresses a critical unmet need: not only forecasting disruptions, but recommending actionable mitigation strategies backed by causal reasoning. By integrating prediction, explanation, and intervention optimization into a continuous-time causal framework, CT-SCaLE establishes a new direction for supply chain analytics, enabling more resilient and adaptive global operations.

segments.label: human

segments.text: Global supply chains have evolved into tightly interconnected, multi-tier networks in which localized disruptions can rapidly escalate into systemic failures. Recent years have shown that cascading failures are no longer rare, slow-moving anomalies, but high-velocity phenomena driven by geopolitical tensions, extreme climate events, pandemics, and infrastructure shocks. Trade restrictions, port closures, energy shortages, and regional conflicts now propagate across borders within days rather than months, overwhelming traditional risk buffers and recovery mechanisms [1], [2]. Empirical studies of global shipping, commodity trade, and critical materials supply chains demonstrate that disruptions often trigger nonlinear ripple effects, amplifying losses far beyond the initially affected nodes [3]–[5]. While organizations increasingly invest in resilience strategies, most responses remain reactive in nature, activating only after disruptions are observed, rather than
segments.label: ai_generated

segments.text: proactively suppressing failure cascades before they materialize [6], [7]. This growing mismatch between disruption speed and decision latency highlights an urgent need for predictive frameworks that can anticipate cascading failures early and guide timely intervention. A substantial body of research has applied machine learning and network analytics to supply chain risk prediction, leveraging graph-based representations to model inter-firm dependencies and disruption propagation [8]–[10]. However, most graph machine learning approaches remain fundamentally correlation-driven, learning statistical associations rather than causal mechanisms governing failure transmission. Even recent advances in causal graph neural networks typically rely on static directed acyclic graphs, implicitly assuming that causal relationships are time-invariant and acyclic [17], [18]. Such assumptions are misaligned with real supply chains, where causal influence strengths evolve over time, feedback loops are common, and disruption pathways change dynamically in response to interventions. Discrete-time modeling further limits responsiveness by aggregating events into coarse temporal windows, causing early-stage cascades to be missed or detected too late [11], [12]. Moreover, counterfactual reasoning in existing models is often applied post hoc—used to explain predictions after the fact—rather than being integrated into an optimization framework that actively identifies and evaluates preventive interventions under cost and timing constraints [15], [16]. As a result, prevailing methods struggle to support real-time, decision-oriented mitigation of cascading failures. To address these limitations, this paper introduces CT-SCaLE, a Continuous-Time Structural Causal Learning Engine for predicting and mitigating cascading failures in global supply chains. Unlike prior approaches, CT-SCaLE jointly learns both the evolving causal topology of supply chain networks and the continuous-time dynamics governing disruption propagation. The framework leverages Neural Ordinary Differential Equations to model high-frequency temporal evolution, enabling the representation of time-varying causal influence, delayed effects, and feedback-driven escalation. Causal structure learning is embedded end-to-end, allowing the model to adapt its causal graph as network conditions change. Crucially, CT-SCaLE is intervention-aware: counterfactual reasoning is integrated directly into the learning and decision pipeline, enabling the simulation and evaluation of proactive mitigation strategies rather than retrospective explanations. By unifying prediction, causality, and intervention planning within a continuous-time framework, CT-SCaLE is designed to meet the operational demands of modern, disruption-prone supply chains. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows: ●​ Continuous-time causal topology learning: We propose a dynamic causal learning mechanism that captures time-varying influence strengths and feedback loops beyond static DAG representations. ●​ Unified cascade prediction and intervention modeling: CT-SCaLE integrates disruption forecasting with multi-step intervention simulation in a single differentiable architecture.

segments.text: ●​ Counterfactual contrastive representation learning: The model learns representations that are explicitly sensitive to intervention outcomes, improving robustness under hypothetical scenarios. ●​ Cost-aware cascading failure mitigation: An embedded intervention planner identifies minimum-cost actions capable of suppressing or redirecting disruption cascades before large-scale propagation occurs. Together, these contributions advance supply chain analytics from passive risk prediction toward continuous-time, causality-driven control of cascading failures, addressing a critical gap in current resilience methodologies.

segments.text: II Literature Review 2.1 Cascading Failures and Systemic Risk in Supply Chains
segments.label: human

segments.text: Global supply chains exhibit strong interdependencies that make them inherently vulnerable to cascading failures, where localized disruptions propagate across tiers and regions. Early system-focused studies highlight how national emergencies—including pandemics, climate disasters, cyber incidents, and geopolitical conflicts—can simultaneously impact multiple supply chain layers, leading to severe shortages and logistical bottlenecks (Khan et al., 2022) [1]. These systemic risks are amplified as firms increasingly adopt outsourcing and lean operating models, enhancing efficiency at the expense of robustness. Yang et al. (2021) [2] formally analyzed this phenomenon by modeling underload-driven cascading failures, demonstrating that demand shocks can trigger disproportionate system-wide collapse, even when recovery mechanisms such as safety stock and backup suppliers are in place. Network-based cascading failure models have since been applied to large-scale physical and trade networks. Xu et al. (2024) [3] investigated port-level disruptions in the Global Container Shipping Network, showing that single-node failures can induce widespread traffic redistribution and overload effects across marine logistics systems. Similar cascading dynamics have been observed beyond logistics, including in resource and waste trade systems. Li et al. (2021) [5] analyzed the collapse of the global plastic waste trade, revealing that capacity overloads propagate through international trade networks unless coordinated mitigation strategies are adopted. These studies collectively confirm that cascading failures are nonlocal, nonlinear, and strongly dependent on network structure—yet they largely rely on static simulations rather than predictive learning.
segments.label: ai_generated

segments.text: 2.2 Ripple Effect Analysis and Recovery-Focused Strategies
segments.label: human

segments.text: Complementary research has explored the ripple effect by simulating how disruptions spread through multi-echelon supply chains and evaluating post-disruption recovery tactics. KEk et al. (2022) [4] used discrete-event simulation to examine disruption propagation in the copper industry, identifying insufficient safety stock and limited sourcing flexibility as primary amplification factors. Manupati et al. (2022) [6] further examined recovery strategies in complex supply chain networks, integrating blockchain-enabled smart contracts and genetic-algorithm optimization to evaluate both pre- and post-disruption decision-making. While these approaches provide valuable managerial insights, they primarily focus on
segments.label: ai_generated

segments.text: response optimization after disruptions occur, rather than anticipating and suppressing cascades during their early evolution. From an organizational and managerial perspective, Park and Singh (2023) [7] emphasized the importance of risk alert tools enabled by big data analytics, showing empirically that robust IT and analytics capabilities significantly enhance firms’ ability to predict risks. However, such alert tools typically operate as early-signal detectors and do not explicitly model how risks propagate across interconnected supply networks. Similarly, resilience reviews across industries—including automotive, pharmaceuticals, shipping, and semiconductors—stress the need for proactive and adaptive mitigation strategies, yet stop short of offering integrated causal-dynamic prediction frameworks (Maheshwari & Jaggi, 2024 [10]; Xiong et al., 2025 [11]).

segments.text: 2.3 Data-Driven Risk Prediction and Digital Supply Chain Surveillance
segments.label: human

segments.text: With the growing availability of heterogeneous digital data, machine learning and artificial intelligence have become central to supply chain risk analytics. Brintrup et al. (2024) [12] introduced the concept of Digital Supply Chain Surveillance, highlighting how AI can uncover hidden dependencies and improve visibility across opaque supplier networks. Related work has leveraged IoT data and deep learning to predict logistics failures under natural hazards, achieving high predictive accuracy but relying largely on black-box sequence models (Alzahrani & Asghar, 2023 [13]). Fraud detection studies further illustrate the effectiveness of ML in identifying anomalous transactions and operational irregularities, though they emphasize correlation-based detection rather than causal intervention planning (Lokanan & Maddhesia, 2025 [8]). System-level modeling approaches have also been developed to assess infrastructure-supply chain interdependencies. Oliver et al. (2022) [15] combined model-based systems engineering with discrete-event simulation to evaluate how infrastructure disruptions affect critical supply chains. Analogous cascading failure studies in power and smart grid networks demonstrate that accounting for heterogeneous component roles and interdependencies improves failure prediction accuracy (Salehpour et al., 2022 [16]; Ghasemi et al., 2023 [20]). Despite methodological advances, these frameworks remain domain-specific and lack generalizable learning mechanisms for evolving causal structures.

segments.text: 2.4 Graph Neural Networks and Network-Aware Prediction Models
segments.label: human

segments.text: Graph-based learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for modeling inter-firm dependencies and disruption propagation. Yang et al. (2024) [18] applied graph neural networks (GNNs) to predict post-hazard firm-level sales changes, demonstrating that incorporating inter-firm relations significantly improves predictive performance over non-network baselines. Kosasih and Brintrup (2022) [19] further extended GNNs with neurosymbolic reasoning to uncover hidden supply chain relationships, enhancing structural visibility. These methods confirm the value of relational learning but are primarily designed for static or discrete-time analysis and do not explicitly model causal dynamics.

segments.text: Recent studies increasingly recognize that predictive accuracy alone is insufficient for effective risk mitigation. Wyrembek et al. (2025) [17] argued that causal machine learning is essential for intervention planning, enabling decision-makers to evaluate “what-if” scenarios under different managerial actions. However, existing causal GNN approaches typically employ fixed or slowly changing causal graphs, assume acyclic relationships, and conduct counterfactual analysis as a post-processing step rather than integrating it into dynamic decision optimization.

segments.text: 2.5 Research Gap and Motivation
segments.label: human

segments.text: Across the literature, three limitations persist. First, cascading failure studies rely heavily on static simulation models that lack predictive and adaptive capabilities. Second, machine learning and GNN-based methods largely capture correlations or static network effects, struggling with time-varying causality and feedback loops. Third, causal and counterfactual approaches remain detached from real-time intervention optimization, limiting their utility for proactive cascade suppression. These gaps motivate the development of a continuous-time, causality-driven learning framework that can jointly predict disruption propagation and optimize mitigation actions—forming the foundation of the proposed CT-SCaLE model.

segments.text: The experimental evaluation of CT-SCaLE is conducted using SupplyGraph, a real-world benchmark dataset designed specifically for graph-based supply chain planning tasks. The dataset represents a multi-tier supply chain network derived from a large fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) enterprise, where nodes correspond to operational entities such as factories, processing units, and distribution centers, while directed edges capture material flow and operational dependencies between them. In this study, we utilize a connected subgraph comprising 1,842 nodes and 4,976 directed edges, selected to reflect realistic multi-echelon interactions while maintaining computational tractability for continuous-time modeling. Each node is associated with 12 time-dependent features, including sales indicators, production levels, and operational stress signals, recorded at daily resolution. These temporal node attributes make the dataset well-suited for modeling disruption evolution and cascading effects over time. A temporal split strategy is adopted to ensure realistic evaluation and prevent information leakage. The first 70% of the time horizon is used for training, the subsequent 15% for validation, and the remaining 15% for testing. This setup reflects real-world deployment conditions, where models must forecast future disruptions using only historical observations. segments.text: 6.7 Discussion
segments.label: human

segments.text: The results demonstrate that modeling supply chain disruptions through continuous-time causal dynamics provides a substantial advantage over traditional discrete and correlation-based approaches. By capturing how causal influence evolves at fine temporal granularity, CT-SCaLE identifies high-risk propagation paths earlier and enables interventions at the moment they are most effective. For managers, this translates into actionable early-warning signals, reduced reaction delays, and more cost-efficient allocation of mitigation resources across multi-tier networks. Unlike black-box predictive systems, the framework’s learned causal structure and counterfactual simulations offer transparent explanations of why disruptions spread and how targeted actions reshape outcomes, supporting evidence-based decision-making. Importantly, CT-SCaLE is designed for deployment realism: it accommodates incomplete visibility, asynchronous updates, and heterogeneous data streams typical of global supply chains, making it suitable for integration into enterprise risk dashboards and real-time monitoring systems. Collectively, these capabilities position continuous-time causal learning as a practical and strategically valuable direction for resilient supply chain operations.

segments.text: 6.8 Limitations and Future Work
segments.label: human

segments.text: Although CT-SCaLE demonstrates strong predictive and intervention capabilities, its performance may be affected by data sparsity in multi-tier supply chains, where incomplete visibility can limit the accuracy of learned causal relationships. Additionally, continuous-time causal identifiability remains challenging in settings with strong confounding or rapidly shifting external conditions, suggesting the need for richer multimodal data integration. Future work will focus on improving real-time deployment efficiency, including adaptive updating, streaming inference, and scalable causal structure learning to support continuous monitoring of large, dynamic global networks.

segments.text: VI Conclusion
segments.label: human

segments.text: This work introduced CT-SCaLE, a continuous-time causal learning framework that integrates prediction, explanation, and intervention planning for cascading failures in global supply chains. Unlike discrete or correlation-based models, CT-SCaLE captures evolving causal influence and fast disruption propagation, enabling more proactive risk management. Experiments show that the model improves prediction accuracy by 14.7%, extends early-warning lead time by 22%, and reduces cascade size by 31.4%, clearly outperforming advanced baselines. By linking causal reasoning with real-time intervention optimization, CT-SCaLE shifts supply chain analytics from forecasting toward actionable, control-oriented resilience. Future efforts will focus on improving causal identifiability under sparse data, enhancing multimodal integration, and optimizing real-time deployment for large-scale industrial networks.
